title: The world watched the first Moon walk through a camera filming a TV screen

cover.alt: Ghostly black-and-white TV image from the Moon: the leg and ladder of the lunar module in the foreground, with the bright, sunlit lunar surface beyond.

body: Apollo 11’s camera on the Moon sent a black-and-white **slow-scan** picture, 10 frames a second with 320 lines, which ordinary television sets could not show. At the receiving stations, a converter displayed it on a 10-inch monitor and a broadcast camera simply re-filmed that screen. Each step lost contrast, brightness and detail, and wrong converter settings at Goldstone in the first minutes left Armstrong barely visible on the ladder. The better-quality original recordings were never found.

slides.alt: Ghostly black-and-white TV footage: beside the lunar module’s leg and ladder, an astronaut walks into the sunlight and flares bright white, then passes close to the camera as a blurred, smeared shape.
slides.caption: The restored broadcast, 20 July 1969: by the lunar module’s ladder, an astronaut walks into sunlight and flares white, then passes close as a smeared ghost.

slides.heading: From the Moon to living rooms

steps.label: The lunar camera sends slow-scan TV
Dishes in California and Australia catch it
A converter shows it on a 10-inch monitor
A TV camera re-films that screen
Relayed on via Houston and New York

slides.question: Why was Armstrong barely visible in the first minutes, as he came down the ladder?
slides.explanation: The scan converter at Goldstone was set wrongly at first. Every analogue link afterwards, through Houston and New York, added more noise.

slides.prompt: What happened to the tapes of the original, sharper slow-scan signal?
slides.answer: They were probably wiped and reused
slides.detail: A 2006–2009 search concluded the one-inch data tapes were most likely erased and reused in the early 1980s, during a tape shortage. NASA restored the best broadcast copies instead.
